findings.title: CIMA new AML Rule and Sanctions Rule — mandatory compliance deadline September 18, 2026
findings.summary: On July 20, 2026, CIMA published a new Rule on Effective Compliance Programme for the Prevention and Detection of Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Proliferation Financing and a new Rule on Compliance with Financial Sanctions and Targeted Financial Sanctions. Both rules apply to all CIMA registered or licensed financial service providers including all registered investment funds. The rules enter into force September 18, 2026.
findings.client_impact: All Cayman investment funds and their CIMA-licensed service providers must have updated AML compliance programmes and sanctions screening procedures in place by September 18, 2026; clients with Cayman fund structures should immediately confirm readiness with their Cayman fund administrators and directors.
findings.urgency_reason: Hard regulatory deadline is September 18, 2026 — 25 days from today. Non-compliance exposes funds and service providers to CIMA enforcement action including suspension or revocation of registration.

findings.title: Luxembourg subscription tax transition period ends August 31, 2026 — MyGuichet.lu filing becomes mandatory
findings.summary: The two-year transition period introduced by AED Circular N°821 (October 2024) for subscription tax returns ends August 31, 2026. From September 1, 2026, use of the new digital filing forms on MyGuichet.lu becomes mandatory for UCIs, SIFs and RAIFs. Filers must provide additional information compared to the previous system; RAIF compartment identifiers (CSSF/ISIN codes) are now obtainable.
findings.client_impact: Luxembourg UCIs, SIFs and RAIFs must file subscription tax returns exclusively via new digital MyGuichet.lu forms from September 1, 2026; any filing attempted through the old system after August 31 will be rejected, potentially triggering penalties and disrupting fund operations.
findings.urgency_reason: Hard deadline is August 31, 2026 — seven days away. Luxembourg fund administrators must confirm their filing systems are updated to the new MyGuichet.lu forms immediately to avoid rejected filings.

findings.title: Cayman Islands DITC closing CRS XML portal for transition to CRS XML Schema v3.0
findings.summary: The Cayman Islands DITC Portal closed for submission of CRS XMLs and Filing Declarations in early August 2026 to accommodate the transition to CRS XML Schema v3.0 (CRS 2.0, in force from January 1, 2026). The CRS 2.0 regime brings digital assets — including e-money wallets, CBDCs, crypto derivatives, and stablecoins — into CRS reporting scope. The DITC will no longer provide an XML generator tool.
findings.client_impact: Cayman-based fund administrators and financial institutions must source their own CRS XML generation tools for the v3.0 format; additionally, clients with Cayman funds that hold or administer digital assets will for the first time have those assets reported under CRS, expanding the information exchange footprint.
findings.urgency_reason: Portal closure occurred in early August 2026; administrators who have not yet sourced alternative CRS XML tooling are already in a compliance gap ahead of Cayman reporting deadlines (deadline moving to June 30, 2027).

findings.title: FINMA implementing major AML Ordinance update for 2026 — enhanced beneficial ownership transparency
findings.summary: FINMA is implementing a major update to the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance for 2026, with a focus on beneficial ownership transparency and strict risk-based supervision. The update reinforces FINMA's supervisory approach and aligns with FATF recommendations on identifying and verifying ultimate beneficial owners across the Swiss financial centre.
findings.client_impact: Swiss financial intermediaries serving HNW clients will face enhanced UBO identification and verification requirements under the updated FINMA AML framework, likely triggering new or refreshed KYC requests for clients with Swiss banking or asset management relationships.
findings.urgency_reason: Developing regulation being implemented through 2026; no single hard deadline identified, but clients with Swiss accounts or advisors should anticipate enhanced due diligence requests and proactively gather UBO documentation.

findings.title: UAE FTA Decision No. 12 of 2026 sets Pillar Two registration and filing deadlines — CT return due September 30, 2026
findings.summary: Issued July 16, 2026, UAE Federal Tax Authority Decision No. 12 of 2026 establishes registration, deregistration and scope-notification deadlines for entities affected by the UAE domestic minimum top-up tax (Pillar Two). The UAE implements the global 15% minimum tax on MNEs with revenues over €750 million. Corporate tax returns for December 2025 year-ends are due September 30, 2026.
findings.client_impact: UAE entities within multinational groups with revenues exceeding €750 million must register for the domestic minimum top-up tax and file corporate tax returns for their December 2025 year-end by September 30, 2026; affected clients face a 15% top-up tax on UAE income if they are part of a qualifying MNE group.
findings.urgency_reason: September 30, 2026 filing deadline for December 2025 year-end entities is 37 days away; clients with large UAE corporate structures should confirm their Pillar Two scope and registration status immediately if not already completed.

findings.title: Panama Law 526 of 2026 introduces economic substance requirements for foreign passive income — applies from 2027 fiscal year
findings.summary: Enacted May 28, 2026, Panama Law 526 requires entities in multinational groups receiving foreign-source passive income (dividends, interest, royalties, capital gains, real estate income) to demonstrate genuine economic substance in Panama to maintain zero-tax treatment. Entities failing the substance test pay 15% on net taxable income. Panama retains its territorial system but now requires actual rather than merely formal presence, effective from the 2027 fiscal year.
findings.client_impact: Clients using Panama holding companies, foundations or SPVs to receive foreign-source passive income must demonstrate genuine economic substance in Panama from 2027 or face a 15% tax on net passive income, potentially eliminating the primary tax benefit of Panama structures.
findings.urgency_reason: Regime applies from the 2027 fiscal year, but restructuring and substance establishment takes time; clients with Panama structures should commission substance assessments and restructuring analysis in Q4 2026 to meet the new requirements.

findings.title: CRS 2.0 in force from January 1, 2026 — digital assets and crypto brought into automatic reporting scope
findings.summary: CRS 2.0, in force from January 1, 2026, extends the Common Reporting Standard to cover digital assets including e-money wallets, Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) holdings, crypto derivatives, and stablecoin accounts. Jurisdictions are transitioning to the updated XML Schema v3.0 for reporting. FATCA reporting deadlines in Saint Kitts and Nevis remain August 29, 2026; Cayman Islands deadlines are moving to June 30, 2027.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients with digital asset holdings — including crypto wallets, CBDC accounts, stablecoins and crypto derivatives — held through financial institutions in CRS-participating jurisdictions will have those assets automatically reported to their home tax authority from 2026, significantly closing the information gap on digital wealth.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since January 1, 2026 with jurisdictions now migrating XML Schema and first reports being filed; clients who assumed digital assets were outside CRS reporting must urgently reassess their disclosure positions with their tax advisors.

findings.title: FinCEN permanently eliminates BOI reporting for US companies and US persons — effective August 14, 2026
findings.summary: Effective August 14, 2026, FinCEN issued a final rule permanently exempting US person beneficial owners from BOI reporting under the Corporate Transparency Act. Foreign entities that are reporting companies must still report BOI for foreign individual beneficial owners. FinCEN also announced it will delete previously reported information by US persons from the BOI database.
findings.client_impact: US persons and US-domiciled entities are permanently exempt from CTA beneficial ownership reporting, eliminating the compliance burden and associated costs; however, foreign entities with non-US beneficial owners that qualify as reporting companies remain subject to BOI disclosure requirements.
findings.urgency_reason: Rule effective August 14, 2026; US-person clients no longer need to act. Clients with foreign reporting entities should confirm their ongoing obligations remain satisfied.

findings.title: FinCEN BOI final rule published in Federal Register — confirms permanent exemption for US persons
findings.summary: The Federal Register published the Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting Requirement Revision on August 14, 2026. The rule finalises exemptions for US-person beneficial owners and company applicants; foreign reporting companies remain subject to disclosure. This closes the CTA's domestic BOI regime, significantly narrowing compliance obligations for US-domiciled structures.
findings.client_impact: Federal Register publication provides the authoritative legal basis for the permanent US-person BOI exemption; advisors can now rely on the published rule when confirming to clients that their US entities need not file or maintain prior filings.
findings.urgency_reason: Confirmatory publication of the already-effective rule; no additional client action required beyond background awareness.

findings.title: Florida SB 264 foreign buyer real estate restrictions remain in force after November 2025 legal uphold
findings.summary: Florida's Senate Bill 264 (effective July 1, 2023), restricting nationals from seven 'countries of concern' (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Venezuela, Syria) from purchasing real estate, was upheld in November 2025 and continues to be enforceable in 2026. Chinese nationals face a near-total ban; nationals from other six countries face restrictions within 10 miles of military installations or critical infrastructure. Buyers must sign affidavits; violations carry potential property forfeiture and criminal charges.
findings.client_impact: Clients who are nationals of China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Venezuela, or Syria face binding legal restrictions on purchasing Florida real estate; Chinese national clients face a near-total ban and must be advised before any Florida property transaction to avoid forfeiture risk and criminal exposure.
findings.urgency_reason: Existing law, upheld November 2025 and continuing in 2026; no new deadline but critical due diligence point for any affected client considering Florida real estate.

findings.title: BCB/CVM Joint Resolution 13/2024 — non-resident investors must use same instruments as residents, in force since January 1, 2025
findings.summary: In force since January 1, 2025, Article 5 of Joint Resolution BCB/CVM 13/2024 requires non-resident investment to be conducted in the same financial instruments and modalities available to resident investors, with equivalent registration requirements and operational limits. This standardises market access for foreign capital and eliminates prior carve-outs for non-resident investment vehicles.
findings.client_impact: Non-resident clients investing in Brazil can no longer rely on previous carve-outs for foreign investment vehicles and must use standard Brazilian investment instruments with the same registration, reporting and operational limits applicable to residents, increasing administrative requirements for Brazil investment portfolios.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since January 1, 2025; background awareness for clients with existing or planned Brazilian investments — no new deadline but a standing change advisors must factor into Brazil investment structuring.

findings.title: Cayman Islands tokenised fund legislation in force since March 24, 2026
findings.summary: The Mutual Funds (Amendment) Act, 2026 and Private Funds (Amendment) Act, 2026 came into force on March 24, 2026, adding statutory definitions and operating requirements for tokenised mutual and private funds. Tokenised funds may issue digital tokens representing fund interests without triggering the VASP regime; they remain regulated under existing funds legislation with additional obligations. CIMA has supervisory powers over tokenised fund technology and digital token transactions.
findings.client_impact: Cayman fund structures may now issue digital tokens representing fund interests under the existing regulatory framework without triggering VASP registration, providing a new structuring option for clients interested in offering tokenised private fund interests while remaining in the established CIMA-regulated environment.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since March 24, 2026; background awareness for clients or fund managers exploring digital token issuance in Cayman fund structures.

findings.title: BVI beneficial ownership register open to 'legitimate interest' access since April 1, 2026
findings.summary: Following the January 1, 2026 filing deadline (with a moratorium on penalties until March 31, 2026), the BVI register became operational for 'legitimate interest' access from April 1, 2026. The register is not public; entities may apply for exemptions preventing disclosure on legitimate interest grounds, though competent authorities and law enforcement retain full access. Required information includes name, month/year of birth, nationality, and nature of interest.
findings.client_impact: Clients with BVI companies must ensure their beneficial ownership information is filed with the BVI register; while the register is not publicly searchable, competent authorities and law enforcement have unrestricted access, and third parties with a demonstrable legitimate interest may apply for access.
findings.urgency_reason: Register operational since April 1, 2026; clients should confirm filings are current with their BVI registered agents and assess whether an exemption application is warranted for sensitive structures.

findings.title: Luxembourg revised carried interest regime in force from January 1, 2026
findings.summary: Law of January 22, 2026 introduced a revised carried interest regime, retroactive to January 1, 2026. The new framework provides a clearer, more robust and permanent statutory basis for the tax treatment of carried interest in Luxembourg, replacing previous administrative guidance.
findings.client_impact: Fund managers and general partners with Luxembourg private equity or VC fund structures now benefit from a clearer statutory carried interest tax treatment, reducing legal uncertainty and potentially improving Luxembourg's attractiveness as a fund domicile for clients launching new fund vehicles.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since January 22, 2026; background awareness for clients with Luxembourg PE/VC structures or those considering Luxembourg for future fund vehicles.

findings.title: MAS announces new carried interest tax exemption and hedge fund investment programme (August 19, 2026)
findings.summary: On August 19, 2026, MAS announced three major measures: a new tax exemption on profit-related returns (carried interest) from fund management services to qualifying funds; a new MAS Hedge Fund Investment Programme to attract top global hedge funds; and a dedicated Investment Management Track under the ONE Pass for investment professionals. Singapore's AUM has grown to approximately S$7 trillion.
findings.client_impact: Singapore is now more competitive for fund managers and GPs seeking a fund domicile or personal residency, with a new carried interest tax exemption and enhanced visa pathway; clients considering Singapore as an alternative to traditional offshore centres should factor these developments into their jurisdiction selection analysis.
findings.urgency_reason: Announced August 19, 2026; positive structural development with no immediate action required but directly relevant for clients exploring Singapore fund platforms or residency strategies.

findings.title: MFSA publishes Financial Crime Compliance Strategy 2026
findings.summary: The Malta Financial Services Authority published its Financial Crime Compliance Strategy 2026, setting out a risk-based and outcomes-driven supervisory model aligned with evolving EU AML/CFT requirements. The strategy covers authorisation, supervision and enforcement stages, directing resources toward higher-risk sectors and activities. It reflects Malta's ongoing alignment with the EU's new AML regulatory package.
findings.client_impact: Malta-based financial service providers and regulated entities serving FGC clients will face more intensive, risk-based AML/CFT supervision; clients with Malta fund structures, insurance solutions or other Malta-licensed vehicles should expect more thorough compliance reviews and potentially enhanced due diligence requests.
findings.urgency_reason: Published August 2026; signals increased Malta AML enforcement intensity throughout 2026 and beyond, but no specific client action deadline identified.

findings.title: Cyprus comprehensive tax reform in force from January 1, 2026 — corporate rate 15%, crypto 8%, reduced SDC
findings.summary: Approved December 22, 2025 and effective January 1, 2026, Cyprus's tax reform raises the corporate income tax rate from 12.5% to 15% (aligning with OECD Pillar Two). A flat 8% tax applies to gains from crypto asset disposals and share-based remuneration. The Special Defence Contribution on dividends was reduced from 17% to 5% for actual distributions. Non-domiciled individuals retain 17-year exemptions on worldwide dividend, interest and investment gains; no estate, inheritance, wealth or gift taxes apply.
findings.client_impact: Cyprus holding structures face a higher corporate tax rate (15%) but the reduced 5% SDC on actual dividend distributions may partially offset the impact; non-domiciled residents retain their extensive exemptions, and the new 8% crypto gains tax requires clients with crypto held through Cyprus entities to reassess their tax position.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since January 1, 2026; clients with Cyprus structures should already have adjusted planning but if not yet done so, a comprehensive Cyprus tax position review is warranted.

findings.title: Bahamas SCB issues DARE Act compliance circular for digital asset custodians — 14-month processing timelines
findings.summary: The Securities Commission of the Bahamas released a supplementary circular addressing DARE Act compliance for digital asset custodians, including segregated custody mandates and quarterly attestation of client asset ringfencing by approved auditors. SCB processing timelines have extended to an average of 14 months as of mid-2026. Applicants must satisfy revised beneficial ownership transparency standards before licences advance.
findings.client_impact: Clients seeking to establish digital asset custodian structures in the Bahamas face 14-month average licensing timelines and must satisfy enhanced beneficial ownership transparency requirements; existing licensed entities must implement segregated custody and quarterly auditor attestations, adding ongoing compliance costs.
findings.urgency_reason: Circular issued August 2026; relevant background for clients exploring Bahamas-based digital asset fund or custody structures — no immediate deadline but lengthy timelines mean planning must begin well in advance.

findings.title: JFSC launches streamlined foreign company continuation process and IP register (July–August 2026)
findings.summary: The Jersey Financial Services Commission launched a streamlined application process for foreign companies continuing into Jersey, including a single form, one payment and clearer guidance, effective July 31, 2026. On August 1, 2026, the JFSC launched Jersey's intellectual property register and myIPO online service. The JFSC also began a consultation on more flexible Handbook requirements for AML reliance arrangements.
findings.client_impact: Clients considering redomiciling foreign holding companies or SPVs to Jersey benefit from a simplified single-application continuation process effective July 31, 2026, reducing administrative friction and cost for cross-border restructurings into the Jersey jurisdiction.
findings.urgency_reason: Effective July 31, 2026; procedural improvement with no immediate client action required but useful intelligence for clients considering Jersey as a restructuring destination.

findings.title: Guernsey GFSC FinReg Quarterly Update — Q2 2026 regulatory changes
findings.summary: Mourant published a summary of Guernsey Financial Services Commission regulatory developments for Q2 2026 (April–June 2026), covering fund regulation, licensing changes, and AML/CFT updates across Guernsey's financial services sector. The update reflects ongoing refinements to Guernsey's regulatory framework aligned with international standards.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Guernsey fund structures should review the Q2 2026 GFSC update with their Guernsey administrators to identify any specific compliance implications arising from the quarter's fund regulation and AML/CFT developments.
findings.urgency_reason: Published Q2 2026; general regulatory awareness update for clients with Guernsey vehicles — no specific deadline identified in this summary.

findings.title: OECD Pillar Two: US exempts domestic companies; ~140 countries adopted; first GIR filings due June 30, 2026
findings.summary: As of August 2026, approximately 140 countries have adopted OECD Pillar Two, with first GloBE Information Return filings for calendar-year taxpayers due June 30, 2026. The US Treasury in January 2026 confirmed US-headquartered companies are exempt from Pillar Two domestically. The January 2026 OECD package introduced simplification measures, new safe harbours and an evidence-based stocktake process.
findings.client_impact: Non-US multinational structures in clients' portfolios remain subject to the 15% global minimum tax in jurisdictions that have adopted Pillar Two; US-headquartered clients are exempt domestically but must account for qualified domestic minimum top-up taxes in other operating jurisdictions — particularly UAE, as noted separately.
findings.urgency_reason: First GIR filing cycle completed June 30, 2026; background awareness for clients with international holding structures — Pillar Two is now the established baseline, requiring ongoing monitoring of adopted jurisdictions.
